metadata.jurisdiction: Supreme Court of India / High Courts
metadata.annotation_method: Extracted from public-domain Indian Supreme Court and statutory texts; independently authored ground-truth points and verified citations.
metadata.dataset_limitations: Benchmark covers major landmark decisions and statutory sections. It is not exhaustive of every state amendment or trial court procedural record.

corpus.text: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act provides that when a contract is broken, if a sum is named as liquidated damages, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named. In Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority (2015), the Supreme Court held that proof of actual loss is essential to award liquidated damages under Section 74, except in rare cases where loss is impossible or difficult to prove.

In Kailash Nath Associates, DDA had forfeited the earnest money of Rs. 78 lakhs deposited by the appellant upon alleged failure to pay the remaining auction price. The Supreme Court found that DDA subsequently re-auctioned the plot for Rs. 11.78 crores—far higher than the appellant's bid of Rs. 3.12 crores. Since DDA suffered no loss, forfeiture of earnest money under Section 74 was held unlawful and arbitrary.

In ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd (2003) 5 SCC 705, the Supreme Court held that if the terms of the contract are clear and unambiguous regarding genuine pre-estimated damages, the court is competent to award the stipulated sum without calling upon the party to prove actual loss. The court also held that patent illegality in an arbitral award constitutes a violation of public policy under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

In Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) 3 SCC 49, the Supreme Court clarified the scope of 'public policy of India' under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996. It held that an arbitral award can be set aside only on grounds such as fundamental policy of Indian law, interest of India, justice or morality, or patent illegality appearing on the face of the award. The court emphasized that the merits of an award cannot be re-opened in a Section 34 petition.

In Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI (2019) 15 SCC 131, the Supreme Court examined the 2015 Amendment to Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court followed Associate Builders but ruled that after the 2015 amendment, 'patent illegality' is no longer available to challenge international commercial arbitrations seated in India, and the test of public policy is strictly narrowed to fundamental policy of Indian law and basic notions of morality or justice.

In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, a unanimous nine-judge Constitution Bench held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. The court expressly overruled previous judgments in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1964) to the extent that they held privacy was not a constitutionally protected right.

In Puttaswamy, the court established a strict three-fold proportionality test for any state encroachment upon privacy: (i) legality (existence of a law), (ii) legitimate state aim or need, and (iii) proportionality of the means adopted to the object sought to be achieved, ensuring the measure is the least intrusive option.

In M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954) SCR 1077, an eight-judge bench held that search warrants under Section 96 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not violate Article 19(1)(f) or Article 20(3) of the Constitution, observing that the Indian Constitution does not recognize an express fundamental right to privacy analogous to the Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution.

In Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964) 1 SCR 332, a six-judge bench held that unauthorized domiciliary police visits at night violated personal liberty under Article 21, but the majority rejected the existence of a broader fundamental right to privacy. Subba Rao, J. in his dissenting opinion held that privacy was an integral element of personal liberty.

corpus.text: In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647, the Supreme Court integrated the 'Precautionary Principle' and the 'Polluter Pays Principle' into Indian environmental jurisprudence as essential features of sustainable development under Article 21 of the Constitution. The court held that polluting tanneries must pay compensation to affected citizens and fund environmental remediation.

corpus.text: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) 1 SCC 395, the Supreme Court articulated the doctrine of 'Absolute Liability' for hazardous and inherently dangerous industrial enterprises. The court expressly distinguished the English rule of Strict Liability in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), ruling that absolute liability is not subject to any exceptions such as act of God or third-party interference.

metadata.case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India

corpus.text: In P. Chidambaram v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2019) 9 SCC 24, the Supreme Court laid down the judicial 'Triple Test' for regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: (1) flight risk, (2) tampering with evidence, and (3) influencing witnesses. The court reiterated that bail is the rule and jail is the exception even in economic offences, unless the triple test is breached.

In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684, the Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of capital punishment under Section 302 IPC, but circumscribed its imposition strictly to the 'rarest of rare cases' where the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. The court mandated balancing aggravating circumstances of the crime against mitigating circumstances of the offender.

metadata.case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab

corpus.text: In Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470, the Supreme Court applied and structured the Bachan Singh rarest of rare doctrine into five clear categories: (i) manner of commission of murder (extreme brutality), (ii) motive (depravity/hire), (iii) antisocial nature (bride burning/caste massacre), (iv) magnitude of crime (mass murders), and (v) personality of victim (child/defenseless).

metadata.case_name: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab

corpus.text: In State of Punjab v. Ram Singh Ex-Constable (1992) 4 SCC 54, the Supreme Court interpreted Rule 16.2(1) of the Punjab Police Rules regarding dismissal for 'gravest acts of misconduct'. The court held that a single lapse or isolated negligent conduct does not automatically qualify as gravest misconduct; there must be intentional, willful disregard of duty or habitual delinquency.

metadata.case_name: State of Punjab v. Ram Singh

corpus.text: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, a thirteen-judge Constitution Bench formulated the 'Basic Structure Doctrine'. The court held that Parliament has wide amending powers under Article 368 of the Constitution, but it cannot amend, alter, or damage the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.

metadata.case_name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

corpus.text: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248, the Supreme Court overruled the narrow interpretation of Article 21 from A.K. Gopalan (1950), ruling that 'procedure established by law' must not be arbitrary, oppressive, or fanciful; it must be just, fair, and reasonable. This introduced substantive due process principles into Indian constitutional law.

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 74, Indian Contract Act 1872: 'Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.'

Statutory Text - Section 34(2), Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996: 'An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only if: (b) the Court finds that: (ii) the arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of India. Explanation 1: An award is in conflict with public policy only if: (i) it was induced by fraud or corruption; (ii) it is in contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law; or (iii) it is in conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice.'

Statutory Text - Section 439, Code of Criminal Procedure 1973: 'Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail: (1) A High Court or Court of Session may direct (a) that any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail, and if the offence is of the nature specified in sub-section (3) of section 437, may impose any condition which it considers necessary for the purposes of that sub-section.'

Exception where loss is impossible or difficult to prove

queries.question: How did the Supreme Court in Kailash Nath reconcile or distinguish ONGC v. Saw Pipes regarding the necessity to prove actual loss for liquidated damages?
queries.expected_answer: Saw Pipes held that genuine pre-estimated damages could be awarded without proving loss when terms are unambiguous. Kailash Nath clarified that proof of loss is required unless it is impossible or difficult to prove, and an injured party cannot claim damages if no loss was suffered.

queries.question: Given that the Supreme Court in Puttaswamy held that privacy is an absolute right that cannot be restricted under any circumstances by Parliament, explain how the government can pass any surveillance laws.
queries.expected_answer: The premise is incorrect. Puttaswamy held that privacy is not an absolute right; it is subject to reasonable restrictions under the three-fold proportionality test (legality, legitimate aim, and proportionality).
